topics.title: Atoms, molecules and the laws of chemical combination

learn.hook: Burn a candle and it seems to vanish. But if you weighed the wax, the oxygen it uses and every bit of gas it gives off, the total mass would not change at all!
points: Law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier): mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Total mass of reactants = total mass of products.
Law of constant proportions (Proust): a pure compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass. Water from any source has hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8.

Dalton's atomic theory explained these laws: all matter is made of tiny atoms; atoms of one element are identical in mass and properties; atoms combine in small whole-number ratios; atoms are neither created nor destroyed in reactions. His idea that atoms are indivisible was later shown to be wrong.
Each element has a symbol, often from its English or Latin name: O for oxygen, Na for sodium (natrium), Fe for iron (ferrum), K for potassium (kalium).

A molecule is the smallest particle of an element or compound that can exist independently. Atomicity is the number of atoms in a molecule: helium (He) is monoatomic, O₂ diatomic, O₃ triatomic. Charged particles are ions: cations are positive and anions are negative.

example.q: Think it through: 3 g of carbon burns completely in 8 g of oxygen. How much carbon dioxide is formed, and which law does this use?
steps: Total mass of reactants = 3 g + 8 g = 11 g.
Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
So the mass of carbon dioxide = 11 g.
This is the law of conservation of mass.
example.answer: 11 g of carbon dioxide; law of conservation of mass.

learn.reallife: Medicine makers rely on the law of constant proportions: a pure compound used in a tablet has the same elements in the same proportion by mass, whichever factory or country it comes from.

games.title: Laws and atoms: true or false?
items: In a chemical reaction, the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products
This is the law of conservation of mass.
Pure water from any source contains hydrogen and oxygen in the same mass ratio
This is the law of constant proportions; the ratio is always 1 : 8.
Modern science agrees that atoms cannot be divided into smaller particles
Atoms contain electrons, protons and neutrons, so Dalton's 'indivisible' idea was wrong.
Helium is a noble gas and is monoatomic.
A molecule of an element contains atoms of different elements
A molecule of an element has atoms of only that element, like O₂.

quiz.q: Which statement is the law of conservation of mass?
options: A compound always has the same elements in the same ratio
Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
quiz.explain: In a chemical reaction the atoms are only rearranged, so the total mass stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the law of conservation of mass with the law of constant proportions

quiz.q: 3 g of carbon combines completely with 8 g of oxygen. What mass of carbon dioxide is formed?
quiz.explain: By the law of conservation of mass, products = reactants = 3 + 8 = 11 g.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts or multiplies the masses instead of adding

quiz.q: Water from a well in Rajasthan and water from a lake in Kashmir are both purified. Which is true about them?
options: The well water has more hydrogen by mass
Their composition depends on the weather
The lake water has more oxygen by mass
Both have hydrogen and oxygen in the same mass ratio, 1 : 8
quiz.explain: By the law of constant proportions, every sample of pure water has hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the source of a pure compound changes its composition

quiz.q: Which idea of Dalton's atomic theory was later shown to be wrong?
options: Atoms of different elements have different masses
quiz.explain: Atoms are made of smaller particles (electrons, protons and neutrons), so they are not indivisible.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the discovery of subatomic particles with Dalton's theory

quiz.q: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
quiz.explain: Sodium's symbol Na comes from its Latin name, natrium. S is sulphur.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every symbol comes from the English name

quiz.q: The symbol Fe stands for which element?
quiz.explain: Fe comes from 'ferrum', the Latin name for iron. Fluorine is F.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the English first letter, picking fluorine

quiz.q: What is the atomicity of ozone (O₃)?
quiz.explain: Atomicity is the number of atoms in one molecule. Ozone has 3 oxygen atoms.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ozone (O₃) with ordinary oxygen (O₂)

quiz.q: A negatively charged ion is called
quiz.explain: Anions carry negative charge, such as Cl⁻. Cations carry positive charge, such as Na⁺.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up cations and anions

teach.ask: Gappu watches wood burn to a small heap of ash: "The ash is so light! Did most of the wood just disappear?"
teach.praise: Chirp! Nothing disappeared: the missing mass went into the air as gases like carbon dioxide and water vapour. Mass is conserved in every chemical reaction!
teach.nudge: If we could catch all the smoke and gases too, would the total mass be less, or the same?

learn.hook: An atom is far too tiny to weigh on any balance. So how do chemists say one oxygen atom is 16 times heavier than one hydrogen atom? They compare!
points: Atoms are too small to weigh directly, so we use relative masses. The standard is the carbon-12 atom.
One atomic mass unit (1 u) is exactly one-twelfth (1/12) of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
Common atomic masses: H = 1 u, C = 12 u, N = 14 u, O = 16 u, Na = 23 u, Mg = 24 u, S = 32 u, Cl = 35.5 u, Ca = 40 u.
Molecular mass = sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule. For example, H₂O = 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 u.
For ionic compounds such as NaCl we use the formula unit mass: 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 u.

example.q: Think it through: Find the molecular mass of sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄. (H = 1 u, S = 32 u, O = 16 u)

learn.reallife: Fertiliser makers calculate molecular masses to know how much nitrogen is in each bag of urea, so farmers know how much to use.

games.title: Lightest to heaviest molecule
games.prompt: Arrange by molecular (or formula unit) mass, smallest first

quiz.q: One atomic mass unit (1 u) is defined as
options: the mass of one hydrogen atom exactly
the mass of one oxygen atom
one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom
quiz.explain: Scientists chose carbon-12 as the standard; 1 u is exactly 1/12 of its mass.
quiz.mistake: Thinks hydrogen is still the standard for atomic mass

quiz.q: What is the molecular mass of water, H₂O, in u? (H = 1, O = 16)
quiz.mistake: Counts only one hydrogen atom

quiz.q: What is the molecular mass of carbon dioxide, CO₂, in u? (C = 12, O = 16)
quiz.mistake: Counts only one oxygen atom, getting 28

quiz.q: What is the molecular mass of ammonia, NH₃, in u? (N = 14, H = 1)
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the nitrogen mass by 3 instead of the hydrogen

quiz.q: What is the molecular mass of sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄, in u? (H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply the oxygen mass by 4

quiz.q: What is the formula unit mass of sodium chloride, NaCl, in u? (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the masses or doubles one of them

quiz.q: What is the formula unit mass of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, in u? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
quiz.mistake: Counts only one oxygen atom, getting 68

quiz.q: Why do chemists use relative atomic masses instead of weighing single atoms in grams?
options: All atoms have the same mass
Grams are not a unit of mass
Atoms are far too tiny to weigh one at a time, so they are compared with a standard atom
quiz.explain: A single atom's mass is extremely small, so it is easier to compare it with one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom.
quiz.mistake: Thinks atoms have no mass because they are invisible

teach.ask: Gappu holds up a glass of water: "How heavy is one water molecule compared with a hydrogen atom? How would you work it out?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Add the atomic masses: 2 hydrogens (1 + 1) and one oxygen (16) make 18 u. So a water molecule is 18 times as heavy as a hydrogen atom!
teach.nudge: How many hydrogen atoms are in one water molecule, and what do I do with their masses?

topics.title: Chemical formulae and the mole concept

learn.hook: Chemists count atoms the way a shopkeeper counts eggs in dozens, but their 'dozen' is a giant number called a mole: about 602 billion trillion!
points: To write a formula, write the symbols (positive ion first), then cross over the valencies. Al (3) and O (2) give Al₂O₃; Mg (2) and Cl (1) give MgCl₂. Polyatomic ions with more than one unit go in brackets: Ca(OH)₂.
Common polyatomic ions: sulphate SO₄²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, hydroxide OH⁻, ammonium NH₄⁺.
One mole of anything contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules or ions). This number is the Avogadro constant.
Molar mass is the mass of one mole in grams; it equals the atomic or molecular mass in u. Water: 18 u, so its molar mass is 18 g.
Number of moles = given mass ÷ molar mass. Number of particles = number of moles × 6.022 × 10²³.

example.q: Think it through: How many moles of water are in 36 g of water, and how many molecules is that?

learn.reallife: Chemists in medicine factories work in moles to make sure every tablet gets exactly the right number of medicine molecules.

games.title: Match the ion to its formula

quiz.q: Aluminium has valency 3 and oxygen has valency 2. What is the formula of aluminium oxide?
quiz.explain: Cross over the valencies: Al gets 2 and O gets 3, giving Al₂O₃.
quiz.mistake: Writes each element's own valency next to it instead of crossing over

quiz.q: What is the formula of magnesium chloride? (Mg valency 2, Cl valency 1)
quiz.explain: Crossing over gives Mg₁Cl₂, written as MgCl₂.
quiz.mistake: Puts the valency of magnesium beside magnesium

quiz.q: What is the formula of calcium hydroxide? (Ca valency 2, OH⁻ valency 1)
quiz.explain: Two hydroxide ions are needed, and the polyatomic ion goes in brackets: Ca(OH)₂.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the brackets, so CaOH₂ wrongly means two hydrogen atoms

quiz.q: How many particles are there in one mole of a substance?
quiz.explain: One mole always contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles, the Avogadro constant.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the mole with a dozen or makes the power negative

quiz.q: How many moles are there in 36 g of water? (Molar mass of water = 18 g)
quiz.explain: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 36 ÷ 18 = 2.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies mass by molar mass or divides the wrong way

quiz.q: What is the mass of 0.5 mole of carbon dioxide (molar mass 44 g)?
quiz.explain: Mass = moles × molar mass = 0.5 × 44 = 22 g.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 0.5 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: What is the molar mass of oxygen gas, O₂? (O = 16 u)
quiz.explain: O₂ has two oxygen atoms: 2 × 16 = 32 u, so its molar mass is 32 g.
quiz.mistake: Uses the atomic mass of oxygen instead of the molecular mass of O₂

quiz.q: Which contains more molecules: 1 mole of hydrogen gas (H₂) or 1 mole of carbon dioxide (CO₂)?
quiz.explain: One mole of any substance has 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Their masses differ, but the counts are the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a heavier substance has more molecules per mole

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: "A mole is an animal that digs holes! What is a mole in chemistry?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! In chemistry, a mole is a counting unit: 6.022 × 10²³ particles, the Avogadro number. And one mole of a substance weighs its molar mass in grams!
teach.nudge: A dozen means 12. What number does a chemist's 'mole' stand for?
